title: Safety barrier visual check and escalation
audience: Pool and spa technicians and cleaners who look at a pool safety barrier before or during a site visit, in any state or territory
learningOutcomes: Complete a visual barrier check covering gaps, gates, latches, climbable objects, doors, windows, locks and covers, and mark any part not seen as not inspected
Explain why a visual check is not a certificate, and say who certifies a barrier in the job's state or territory
Stop water-side work when a barrier defect leaves the water reachable, and escalate through the set path
Write a barrier check record and defect report that use no compliance wording

instruction.heading: Why the barrier check comes first
instruction.body: Its job is to keep very young children away from the water when no adult is watching. The December 2025 WA guide reports 19 fatal and 174 non-fatal drownings of children under five in swimming and spa pools between July 2012 and June 2022. A barrier that is propped open, damaged, bypassed or left unlatched offers little or no protection, even if most of it is sound. A look at the barrier before you start work is therefore part of the job, and what you see is recorded.

instruction.heading: What you may and may not do
instruction.body: This is a visual, non-certifying check. You look for visible defects, record what you can see, and escalate. You do not decide whether a barrier complies with the law. You do not sign, issue or describe any certificate of compliance or non-compliance, and you do not tell an owner or a swimmer that a barrier is safe, compliant or approved. Only the inspector or authority named for the state or territory can inspect and certify a barrier (see “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”). In NSW, the certificates come from councils or registered inspectors. In Victoria, a registered inspector completes a Form 23 barrier compliance certificate. Do not measure a barrier to pass or fail it. Do not adjust a hinge, latch or self-closing device, and do not move, remove or add a barrier part to make the check pass. Those belong to the owner, a licensed or authorised person, or the local permit body, not to you.

instruction.heading: What to look at
instruction.body: Walk the length of the barrier on both sides, where you can safely reach them, and look for these visible conditions. Gaps: any opening you can see through or under, including a gap at the ground, a gap where a panel has gone, or a gap at the gate. Condition: a broken, bent, rotten, rusted or loose section, or a post that moves. Removable parts: any panel, slat or gate fitting that lifts out or comes off without tools. Gates: whether the gate is hung to open away from the water, whether it returns to the shut position when released from a partly open position, and whether the latch engages. Observe these; do not force the gate. Latch release: whether the release sits high on the water side, can be reached over the barrier by a child, or is shielded; record what you see. Locks: a padlock, deadlock or key lock fitted to a gate, door or window in the barrier. Climbable objects: furniture, barbecues, pots, planters, stacked materials, ladders, water features, trees, shrubs, retaining walls, and pumps or filters close enough that a child could step onto them, on either side. Doors and windows: any door or openable window in the barrier wall. Covers: a pool cover, even a lockable one, does not count as a barrier. Above-ground pools: any ladder or steps that can be removed, and any pump or filter near the wall.

instruction.heading: WA reference figures (WA only)
instruction.body: The December 2025 WA guide, Rules for Pools and Spas, supersedes the 2016 edition. Its figures apply in Western Australia only. They are listed here only so that you can recognise an obvious defect, not as a test you can use to certify anything. The guide says that water deeper than 30 cm brings a pool under the barrier rule. It sets a barrier height of 1.2 m or more on the non-poolside, with height measured from the finished ground level. The gap under the barrier and under a gate may not be more than 100 mm. Under the guide's first option, a gate latch release must sit 1500 mm or more above the ground on the non-poolside. The horizontal gap between vertical members may not exceed 100 mm. A self-closing hinge that stands out more than 10 mm can help a child climb, so it must be kept clear of non-climbable zones. A gate should open outward, away from the water, rather than toward it. Check the WA guide itself before relying on any figure. No figures for any other state or territory are given in this course. Check the authority for the job's state in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”.

instruction.heading: The escalation path
instruction.body: Use this path, and stop at the first step that applies. Step 1, immediate danger: if a child or any unsupervised person can reach the water through a gap or an open gate, do not start water-side work. Make the area safe as far as you can without entering the water, tell the owner at once, and call the emergency number if someone is at risk. Step 2, defect found without immediate danger: do not start water-side work while the defect leaves the water reachable. Do not repair the defect yourself unless the work order covers it and you are competent. Step 3, record: write a defect report with the location, what you saw, the time, photographs where your business policy requires them, and the person told. Step 4, business escalation: give the report to the responsible person named in the work order, who decides whether your job continues. Step 5, owner and authority: the owner keeps the barrier working. Tell the owner in writing that a formal inspection or repair is needed, and point them to the authority in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check” for the job's state or territory. Your business escalation contact decides whether any other body is informed. If you refuse to start work, record the refusal, the reason and the person told.

instruction.heading: Records and wording
instruction.body: Every barrier check record states the date, the time, the site, the parts checked, the parts not inspected, and each defect found. The record uses the words visual check, not compliance check. Write what you saw in plain words. Do not write that a barrier is compliant, safe, certified or approved. If any section of the barrier was not visible or could not be reached safely, record it as not inspected. The record shows what you looked at and what you did about it. It is not a certificate.

procedure: Confirm the work order includes the barrier check, and confirm the site classification from “Scope, site classification and authority”.
Confirm the state or territory for the site and the authority listed for it in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”.
Walk the barrier on both sides where it is safe to do so. Note the parts you could not see or reach.
Check gaps at the ground, at the gate and in any removable panel. Do not force any part.
Watch the gate close from a partly open position and note whether the latch engages. Do not adjust it.
Check for climbable objects on both sides, and for doors, windows, locks, covers and removable ladders at or near the barrier.
For each defect, apply the escalation path in this lesson. Do not start water-side work while a defect leaves the water reachable.
Complete the record, listing the parts not inspected and each defect found.
Hand the record to the responsible person before you start the water-side work or leave the site.

workedExamples.situation: A residential pool. The side gate has a broken latch, and a toddler's ride-on toy sits against the outer face of the fence. The owner says the children are old enough to be fine.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The defect and the climbable toy mean the water may be reachable. You do not start water-side work. You tell the owner that the gate needs securing and that a defect has been found. You do not repair the latch unless the work order covers it. You record the broken latch, the toy's position, the time and the owner's reply, and you tell the responsible person. You do not write that the barrier is compliant.

workedExamples.situation: An above-ground pool has a removable ladder, a pool filter sitting against the wall, and a padlock on the gate. The owner asks you to confirm the barrier is fine so they can tell their insurer.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say and write?
workedExamples.reasoning: You record the removable ladder, the filter near the wall and the padlock on the gate, as seen. You do not confirm that the barrier is fine, because you do not certify barriers. You tell the owner that a formal barrier inspection is needed, and that the authority in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check” for the state can advise. The record says visual check only. You do not make statements to the insurer on the owner's behalf.

workedExamples.situation: A commercial spa has a gate that closes but does not latch when released from a half-open position. The operator says the gate was serviced yesterday.
workedExamples.reasoning: You observe and record that the gate does not latch when released from a half-open position, with the time and the operator's statement. You do not adjust the latch, because it is outside the work order and adjustment would be a repair. You escalate to the operator as the responsible person and recommend a formal inspection. Water-side work does not start while the gate defect leaves the pool reachable.

equipmentAndPpe: Barrier check sheet from the business's inspection checklist
Torch for shaded areas and under the barrier
Camera or photo record, where {{business:jobs.photo_requirements}} requires it
Closed footwear with grip, and PPE as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Telling the owner the barrier is compliant or approved.
commonErrors.prevention: Record what was seen. Only the authority or an authorised inspector certifies a barrier.

commonErrors.error: Adjusting a latch, hinge or self-closer to make the gate pass.
commonErrors.prevention: Observe and record. Adjustment belongs to the owner or a qualified person.

commonErrors.error: Treating a padlock or a pool cover as a barrier.
commonErrors.prevention: Neither is a barrier. Record what you see and escalate.

commonErrors.error: Checking only the face of the barrier that looks onto the pool.
commonErrors.prevention: Check both faces of the barrier where it is safe and accessible, and list any face not seen.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a verbal assurance that a defect has been fixed.
commonErrors.prevention: Re-check the item, and record any item you cannot re-check.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not give authority to certify, inspect for legal compliance, or repair a pool safety barrier. Only the inspector or authority named for the state or territory can certify (“Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”).
Drowning risk: never start water-side work while a child or an unsupervised person can reach the water through a barrier defect.
The WA figures in this lesson apply in WA only and come from the December 2025 WA guide; check the guide itself before relying on them.

Each state and territory sets its own barrier rules, and commercial spas may fall under different rules. For the authority and status of each jurisdiction, see “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”. No figures for other states are given here.
Part H7 of NCC 2022 Volume Two, in its performance requirement H7P1, calls for a barrier at swimming pools.

qualityStandard: The check covers both faces of the barrier where it is safe to look, and the record lists the parts not inspected
Each defect is recorded with location, time and the person told, before water-side work resumes
No record or statement describes the barrier as compliant, certified or approved
Any repair or adjustment is referred, not made, unless the work order covers it and the learner is competent
documentationEvidence: Barrier check record with date, time, site, faces checked and parts not inspected
Defect report with location, description, photographs where required, and the person told
Owner response, in writing where possible
Refusal or stop-work record, where applicable
summary: The barrier check is visual and non-certifying. Record what you see; do not judge compliance.
Stop water-side work while a defect leaves the water reachable, and tell the responsible person.
Do not adjust, repair or measure barrier parts to pass them, unless the work order and your competence allow it.
Barrier rules differ by state and territory. Check the authority for the job's site in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”.

knowledgeChecks.question: During a pre-start visit, the side gate is open and a small child is inside the fenced area, on the water side of the gate. What is the correct first action?
options: Start the water-side task, since the child is not in the water yet and the gate can wait
Adjust the gate latch yourself so that it closes properly today and locks
Keep the child away from the water, tell the owner, and do not start water-side work
Note it on the job sheet at the end of the day, then continue the water-side work

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a barrier check record show?
options: That the barrier complies with the state law and all the rules
What was seen, what was not inspected, and any defects and who was told
That the owner will not be fined for the barrier at all today
That the barrier will last for four years before it needs work

knowledgeChecks.question: A pool cover, even a lockable one, is found over the pool. How is it treated in the barrier check?
options: As a barrier, if it is locked and secured with a key at all times
As a barrier, if it is in good condition and well fitted to the pool
As not a barrier, and recorded so that the need for a barrier is escalated
As a barrier only for above-ground pools, not in-ground ones
